org.details: Open Science and Open Source. Creator of Synapse.org, NIH-listed generalist repository for biomedical data managing 2+PB data. Enabler of DREAM biomedical challenges

title: Do incidental findings unrelated to the primary condition fall under the public-repo / CC BY 4.0 requirement?

latest.raw:
A question about the requirement that repositories be made public once the Hackathon ends, with submissions released under CC BY 4.0.

Running an unbiased secondary-findings scan (whole VCF against the full ClinVar Pathogenic/Likely-pathogenic set, reportability judged against ACMG SF v3.2) surfaced a small number of ClinVar P/LP variants the proband carries that are unrelated to the MVA question. None is in an ACMG SF v3.2 gene, so none is reportable under that framework. One is a high-confidence loss-of-function allele in a gene associated with a dominant tumour predisposition. We flagged that one in the submission notes, given this child's existing cancer-predisposition syndrome.

Publishing the causal variants is the point of the exercise. Publishing an unrelated predisposition allele is a different kind of disclosure about a living child, so we would rather ask than assume.

1. Is the public-repository requirement intended to cover incidental findings of this kind, or only the submission and the method?
2. If we should not publish them, what would you prefer: omit them from the repository entirely, or include them in the submitted report for the panel while keeping them out of the public repository?
3. Is there a preferred channel for reporting an incidental finding of potential clinical relevance back to the family's clinical team, or is that explicitly out of scope?

We have kept the repository private in the meantime.

latest.raw:
Hi,

Thank you — genuinely — for how you've handled this. Keeping the repository private, not naming the gene, and asking rather than assuming was exactly the right call, and we don't take that responsibility lightly.

This touches on something beyond what I can answer on my own: whether and how incidental findings of potential clinical significance get returned is governed by the study's IRB protocol and consent terms, not something I can decide ad hoc as a hackathon organizer. I'm escalating your three questions to our Privacy and Compliance Officer and the IRB lead on this project today, given the clinical relevance here.

In the meantime: please keep the repository private, and please don't take any independent action to contact the family or their clinical team directly — not because your instinct is wrong, but because if this does need to go back to them, it needs to happen through the proper consented channel, not an ad hoc one, for their protection as much as anything else.

I know this is an unsatisfying "we'll get back to you," but given what's actually at stake here I'd rather take the time to get this right than give you a fast answer I'm not certain of. I'll follow up as soon as I hear back — thank you for your patience, and for taking this as seriously as you have.

Best,
Gaia
